notes: West 2007 ch. 2 reconstructs the wording, not only the motif: 'There was evidently in MIE an expression "both in word and in deed" or "neither in word nor in deed", based on the alliterating instrumentals *wekʷesh₁ . . . *wergoh₁', citing Il. 1.504, 5.879, Hymn. Dem. 117, Gathic vacaŋhā š́yaoθanācā, Hávamál 141 and Beowulf 1100. Greek keeps both words in the case form of the formula: ἢ ἔπει ἢ ἔργῳ (Il. 1.504; also 1.395, 5.879, Hymn. Hom. 2.65, 2.117, 2.199; all checked in AGDT and glaux). Old English keeps 'deed' and renews 'word' (word < *werdʰom, cognate with Lat. uerbum, not with ἔπος): wordum ne worcum 'neither by words nor deeds', Beowulf 1100, in the Finnsburh treaty (H–S prints it as 1101; Grein's Bibliothek has the same text at 1100, so it is the manuscript reading, not an emendation), and wordum and worcum, Beowulf 1834 (H–S), where Beowulf promises that Hygelac 'will support me by words and deeds' (þæt he mec fremman wile). That is the frame of the Greek prayer formula 'if ever I helped you by word or by deed' (Il. 1.503–504 ὄνησα; 1.395 ὤνησας; Hymn. Dem. 65 ἴηνα), but the verbs are not cognate (ὀνίνημι, fremman), so the record is the merism alone. Avestan keeps 'word' and renews 'deed': Y. 31.22b vacaŋhā š́iiaōϑanācā (CAB, checked), the same X Y-ca shape as the line. So each member is exact in two branches but in different pairs: *wékʷos in Greek and Avestan, *wérǵom in Greek and Old English; only Greek has both. English: 'work', the lexicon's gloss of *wérǵom and the older sense West notes for English work ('in word and work'). Morphology: instrumental singular, as West reconstructs and as Avestan vacaŋhā (*-esh₁) has; the Greek dative ἔπει, ἔργῳ continues the syncretic dative-instrumental, and the OE plurals are the usual Germanic dative-instrumental plural of the idiom. The conjunction -kʷe on the second member follows Avestan -cā and the Greek both-and variant (Hymn. Dem. 117 ἠμὲν … ἠδὲ καί; Il. 15.234, Od. 2.272 ἔργον τε ἔπος τε); the either-or and neither-nor variants of Il. 1.504, 5.879 and Beowulf 1100 are not encoded. Hávamál 141 (orð mér af orði … verk mér af verki) has both Norse words but as two polyptota, not the merism: support only. Caveats: the Phase 8c review (claim C034) graded the Greek/Avestan/OE comparison weak because 'word and deed' is a widespread merism and Germanic keeps one member; this record answers that only by keeping to West's explicit lexical reconstruction and citing the instrumental formula, not the motif. The OE pairing could also be reinforced by Latin uerbo et opere: Grein's other instances (e.g. vordum and veorcum in religious verse) are Christian, so only the two secular Beowulf passages are cited.

West 2007 ch. 2: 'An alternative expression, shared by Greek and Norse, is "come to one's mother's knees": Hes. Th. 460 μητρὸς πρὸς γούναθ' ἵκοιτο; Sigurðarkviða 45 of komz fyr kné móður. It reflects the widespread and ancient practice of giving birth in a kneeling position.' Both passages are about birth: in Hesiod, Kronos swallows each child as it 'came from the holy womb to its mother's knees' (glaux, checked); in the Norse, Hǫgni says of Brynhild hon krǫng of komz fyr kné móður, 'she came to her mother's knees ill-starred', i.e. was born to bring grief (Neckel's text in TITUS, st. 45, and FJ 1926, st. 46, both read kné móður; checked). Both members are cognate: Gk γόνυ = ON kné < *ǵónu, Gk μήτηρ = ON móðir < *méh₂tēr. Case: both daughters put the knees in the accusative after a preposition of direction (πρός + acc., fyr + acc.); the line has the bare accusative of goal, the inherited construction the prepositions were added to. Number: Greek γούνατα is plural; ON kné is formally ambiguous (neuter sg. = pl.) but 'knees' in context. The plural follows Greek, not the dual that the brief's rule for natural pairs would suggest, because no daughter attests a dual here. Forms: the engine's ACC.PL ǵónuh₂ is the handbook u-stem neuter plural in *-uh₂; Gk γούνατα has the Greek -ατ- extension and ON kné the Germanic thematized stem *knewa-, so neither contradicts it. GEN.SG méh₂tr̥s is the zero-grade ending that ON móður (< *-r̥s, like Ved. mātúr) continues; Gk μητρός has the variant *-tr-ós. Greek puts the genitive first, as the line does; Norse puts it after the noun. The verb of the formula is renewed in each branch (Gk ἱκνέομαι, ON koma < *gʷem-) and is not shared, so by the head rule the record is the noun phrase alone; West's paraphrase 'come to …' is the frame, not part of the line. Interpolated: nothing. Only two loci exist (no further instance in Homer, the Hymns, Hesiod or Pindar in glaux with the birth sense; Il. 5.370–371, where Aphrodite falls into the lap of her mother Dione, and Od. 6.310 are a different idiom, supplication or refuge).
